Chapter 9: The Paradoxes of Christianity — Holding Opposites Together.
Life’s never as simple as we’d like, is it? We all feel it—that constant pull in different directions. You want freedom, but you also want to belong. You’re searching for truth, but at the same time, you crave a little mystery.
The old faith—especially with all its paradoxes—offered a way to actually hold these tensions together, instead of pretending they don’t exist.
I remember a friend once, wrestling with doubt, looking me in the eye and asking, "How can you believe in a God who’s both just and merciful? Both all-powerful and yet somehow humble?"
There wasn’t some neat answer or formula to hand over. What I shared was a story—a story of a God who became human, who suffered, died, and then rose again. In that story, the contradictions aren’t erased. They’re embraced.
The old faith taught that the greatest truths are often found in paradox. Think about it: it’s in dying that we find life. In giving, we receive. And in surrendering, somehow, we’re set free.
These aren’t just religious slogans—they’re clues to how life really works.
Most of us don’t even realize how much we need this kind of wisdom. Our modern world loves clarity and control. It pushes us to pick sides, to resolve every tension by choosing one thing over another. But what if we didn’t have to choose?
The old faith invites us to live with open hands. To hold together things that seem to be in conflict, and trust there’s something deeper going on.
Here’s something important: the paradoxes of Christianity aren’t roadblocks to faith—they’re invitations. They call us to look beneath the surface. To see that the world—and maybe even our own lives—are more mysterious, more beautiful, than we ever dared to imagine.
